meta.title: TLS 1.3
meta.summary: How a browser and a web server agree on keys, prove the server's identity and start encrypting, message by message, on top of a TCP connection that is already open (the clock starts after the TCP handshake). Labels use the RFC's brackets: {} sent with handshake keys, [] with application keys, () with early data keys.
meta.source: RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3, including appendix A state names), RFC 8448 (example TLS 1.3 handshake traces), RFC 7301 (ALPN), RFC 6066 (server_name and status_request), RFC 6962 (certificate transparency), RFC 9113 (HTTP/2 preface and SETTINGS)

functional: Agrees on fresh keys with an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman exchange (x25519 or P-256) carried in the ClientHello and ServerHello
Authenticates the server: a certificate chain that leads to a trusted root, then a signature over the whole handshake with the certificate's private key
Protects everything after the ServerHello: extensions, the certificate and both Finished messages travel under handshake keys
Hands out session tickets so the next connection can resume with a pre-shared key, optionally sending its first request in the very first flight (0-RTT)
nonFunctional: One round trip on top of TCP before the client can send its request (TLS 1.2 needed two)
Forward secrecy for every full handshake: stealing the server's long-term key later does not decrypt recorded traffic
0-RTT early data saves a round trip on resumption but is not forward secret and can be replayed, so only idempotent requests belong in it
A wrong key_share guess costs a whole extra round trip (HelloRetryRequest), which is why clients guess the groups servers almost always support
The name of the site (SNI) still goes in the clear unless Encrypted Client Hello is used

scale.label: Full handshake
scale.value: 1 RTT after TCP, so the request leaves at 1 RTT and the response is back at 2

scale.label: Resumption with 0-RTT
scale.value: request in the first flight, response back after 1 RTT

scale.label: HelloRetryRequest
scale.value: 2 RTT before the client can send

nodes.label: Browser
nodes.description: The TLS client: opens the connection, offers what it supports, checks the server's certificate

nodes.label: Web server
nodes.description: The TLS server for www.example.com on port 443: picks the parameters and proves who it is with its certificate and private key

flows.title: Full handshake (1-RTT)
flows.summary: A first connection: one round trip of hellos and the server's encrypted flight, then the client's Finished leaves together with its first request. The server hands out a session ticket at the end.

steps.label: Make an x25519 key pair
steps.detail: The TCP connection to www.example.com:443 is already open (the TCP module shows that round trip), so the clock here starts at zero when TLS begins. The client makes a fresh, single-use key pair for the key exchange. It must guess which group the server will accept; x25519 is the usual first guess. Both sides are in START, the RFC 8446 appendix A name for 'nothing sent yet'.

fields.name: group
fields.note: RFC 8446 9.1: implementations SHOULD support X25519 and MUST support secp256r1

fields.name: private key
fields.note: Ephemeral: thrown away after the handshake, which is what makes forward secrecy possible

fields.name: public key
fields.note: Goes into the key_share extension

steps.label: ClientHello
steps.detail: The client's whole offer in one plaintext message: the versions, cipher suites, groups and signature algorithms it supports, plus a key share for its guessed group, so the server can finish the key exchange in its first reply. The legacy fields keep old middleboxes happy; the real version negotiation happens in supported_versions. The client now waits for the ServerHello (WAIT_SH); when it arrives the server is in RECVD_CH.

fields.name: message
fields.note: Handshake type client_hello (1)

fields.name: protection
fields.note: No keys exist yet: anyone on the path can read every field

fields.name: legacy_version
fields.note: Says TLS 1.2 on purpose; TLS 1.3 is offered in supported_versions

fields.name: legacy_session_id
fields.note: Non-empty only for middlebox compatibility mode (appendix D.4); the server echoes it

fields.name: cipher_suites
fields.note: In 1.3 a suite names only the record cipher and the hash; key exchange and signatures are negotiated separately

fields.name: supported_groups
fields.note: Every group the client could use, in preference order

fields.name: key_share
fields.note: A share only for the guessed group; a wrong guess costs a HelloRetryRequest

fields.name: signature_algorithms
fields.note: What the client accepts in CertificateVerify and in certificates

fields.name: server_name (SNI)
fields.note: In the clear, so the server can pick the right certificate; an observer sees it too

fields.name: ALPN
fields.note: RFC 7301: the application protocols the client can speak, in preference order

fields.name: psk_key_exchange_modes
fields.note: Tells the server which kind of session ticket the client will accept: PSK combined with a fresh (EC)DHE

steps.label: Pick parameters
steps.detail: The server picks from the client's lists: TLS 1.3, a cipher suite, the x25519 group (the client already sent a share for it, so no retry is needed), a certificate for www.example.com that matches the client's signature algorithms, and h2 from the ALPN list. It is now NEGOTIATED.

fields.name: cipher_suite
fields.note: The mandatory-to-implement suite; SHA-256 is the transcript and key schedule hash from now on

fields.name: certificate
fields.note: Chosen by SNI and signature_algorithms

steps.label: Derive handshake keys
steps.detail: The server makes its own x25519 key pair, combines its private key with the client's public share and gets the shared secret. That goes into the key schedule (HKDF) with a hash of the transcript so far, ClientHello and the ServerHello it is about to send, and out come one handshake traffic secret per direction. Everything it sends after the ServerHello is encrypted with these.

fields.name: (EC)DHE shared secret
fields.note: The same value the client will compute from the other two halves; never sent

steps.label: ServerHello
steps.detail: The only server message in the clear. It carries the server's choices and its own key share. When it arrives (1 RTT) the client can compute the same shared secret and the same handshake keys, so it moves to WAIT_EE: everything after this is encrypted. Its random value also carries the downgrade check: if the server had negotiated TLS 1.2 or lower, the last 8 bytes would spell DOWNGRD.

fields.name: message
fields.note: Handshake type server_hello (2)

fields.name: random
fields.note: For TLS 1.3 the last 8 bytes are random; 44 4F 57 4E 47 52 44 01 would mean the server was pushed down to TLS 1.2

fields.name: supported_versions
fields.note: This, not legacy_version, is what says TLS 1.3

steps.label: Derive handshake keys
steps.detail: The client computes X25519(client private, server public), the same shared secret, and runs the same key schedule over the same transcript. Now it can decrypt the rest of the server's flight, which was sent right behind the ServerHello and arrives with it. In middlebox compatibility mode a dummy change_cipher_spec record also arrives here and is ignored.

fields.name: keys
fields.value: client and server handshake traffic secrets
fields.note: Each expands into an AES-128-GCM key and IV for one direction

steps.label: {EncryptedExtensions}
steps.detail: The server's answers to the client's extensions that are not needed for the key exchange, now hidden from observers: the chosen application protocol and an empty server_name to say it used the SNI. In TLS 1.2 these sat in the plaintext ServerHello.

fields.name: message
fields.note: Handshake type encrypted_extensions (8)

fields.name: protection
fields.note: On the wire the record says application_data (23); the real type is inside the encryption

fields.name: ALPN
fields.note: HTTP/2 will run on this connection

fields.name: server_name
fields.note: An empty extension: 'I used your SNI'

steps.label: {Certificate}
steps.detail: The certificate chain: the leaf for www.example.com first, then the intermediate that signed it. The root is not sent; the client must already have it. In TLS 1.3 this is encrypted, so a passive observer no longer sees which certificate the server presented.

fields.name: message
fields.note: Handshake type certificate (11)

fields.name: certificate_request_context
fields.note: Zero length for a server certificate; it only matters for client certificates

fields.name: certificate_list[0]
fields.note: The leaf, DER-encoded X.509

fields.name: certificate_list[1]
fields.note: Signed by a root in the client's trust store

fields.name: entry extensions
fields.note: OCSP stapling: in TLS 1.3 the response rides in the leaf's CertificateEntry, only if the client asked for it

steps.label: Check the chain
steps.detail: The client builds a path from the leaf through the intermediate to a root it already trusts, checks every signature on the way, checks that today is inside each certificate's validity dates, that the leaf's subjectAltName covers www.example.com, and the revocation and certificate transparency evidence its policy requires. Shown as one step after the message for clarity; implementations do this while processing the Certificate.

fields.name: path
fields.value: leaf -> Example Intermediate CA -> trusted root
fields.note: Each certificate's signature checks out with the next one's public key

fields.name: name
fields.note: Modern clients match the SAN, not the CN

fields.name: validity
fields.value: notBefore <= now <= notAfter, for every certificate

fields.name: result
fields.value: trusted, but not yet proven to be this server's
fields.note: Anyone can replay a certificate; the next message proves possession of the private key

steps.label: {CertificateVerify}
steps.detail: A signature with the certificate's private key over a hash of the whole handshake so far. It proves the server holds the key for the certificate it just sent, and because the transcript includes both key shares, it also proves no one swapped them.

fields.name: message
fields.note: Handshake type certificate_verify (15)

fields.name: signed content
fields.note: The prefix and context string stop the signature being reused anywhere else

steps.label: Check the signature
steps.detail: The client checks the signature with the public key from the leaf certificate it just validated. If it verifies, the party at the other end holds www.example.com's private key.

steps.label: {Finished}
steps.detail: A MAC over the entire handshake with a key derived from the server's handshake secret. It confirms the server saw exactly the same messages as the client. This closes the server's first flight: ServerHello to Finished all left together. With no client certificate requested, the server goes through WAIT_FLIGHT2 to WAIT_FINISHED.

fields.name: message
fields.note: Handshake type finished (20)

fields.name: verify_data
fields.note: 32 bytes with SHA-256; finished_key = HKDF-Expand-Label(server_handshake_traffic_secret, "finished", "", 32)

steps.label: Derive app keys
steps.detail: The transcript through its own Finished is enough for the server to derive the application traffic secrets. It did not ask for a client certificate, so it moves on from WAIT_FLIGHT2 to WAIT_FINISHED and waits only for the client's Finished.

steps.label: [SETTINGS] 0.5-RTT data
steps.detail: The server may send application data right after its Finished, before it hears from the client (0.5-RTT data, RFC 8446 section 2). Here it is the HTTP/2 server preface, a SETTINGS frame. The catch: the server has not yet seen the client's Finished, so it has no proof the client is live or saw the same handshake, and if client certificates were in use it would not yet know who the client is. So this data must not depend on who the client is.

fields.name: message
fields.note: HTTP/2 SETTINGS frame, the server's connection preface (RFC 9113 3.4)

fields.name: SETTINGS
fields.note: Example values; each server picks its own

steps.label: Check Finished, derive app keys
steps.detail: The client checks the server's Finished MAC against its own transcript, then derives the same application traffic secrets. Its next message, Finished, takes it to CONNECTED. It sends that at 1 RTT, and it does not need to wait for anything else before sending its request.

fields.name: server Finished
fields.note: Otherwise abort with decrypt_error

fields.name: keys
fields.value: client and server application traffic secrets

steps.label: {Finished}
steps.detail: The client's own MAC over the transcript, still under the client handshake keys. It leaves at 1 RTT and arrives at 1.5. When it checks out, the server is CONNECTED too and knows the handshake was not tampered with. In compatibility mode a dummy change_cipher_spec record goes just before it.

fields.name: message
fields.note: Handshake type finished (20)

fields.name: verify_data
fields.note: finished_key from client_handshake_traffic_secret

steps.label: [GET /]
steps.detail: The first request goes in the same flight as the client's Finished (delay 0), so it reaches the server at 1.5 RTT: one round trip of TLS on top of TCP's one. It opens with the HTTP/2 client preface and SETTINGS, then the request on stream 1.

fields.name: message
fields.note: HTTP/2 preface, SETTINGS, then a HEADERS frame on stream 1

steps.label: [NewSessionTicket]
steps.detail: After the client's Finished, the server sends a ticket for the next connection. The PSK it stands for is derived from the resumption secret, whose transcript includes the client's Finished, which is why the RFC lets the server send it only after it has received the client's Finished (section 4.6.1). The early_data extension says the next connection may use 0-RTT. A server may send several, for example so a browser can open parallel connections later; each should be used once.

fields.name: message
fields.note: Handshake type new_session_ticket (4), a post-handshake message

fields.name: ticket_lifetime
fields.note: Example value: one day. The RFC caps it at 604,800 s (7 days)

fields.name: ticket_age_add
fields.note: Hides the ticket's age on the wire when it is used

fields.name: ticket_nonce
fields.note: PSK = HKDF-Expand-Label(resumption_master_secret, "resumption", ticket_nonce, 32)

fields.name: ticket
fields.note: A lookup key or the server's own encrypted state; the client cannot read it

fields.name: early_data
fields.note: Example value: how many bytes of 0-RTT data the server will take

steps.label: [200 OK]
steps.detail: The response, sent right behind the ticket. It reaches the client 2 RTT after TLS started, 3 RTT after the TCP SYN.

fields.name: message
fields.note: HTTP/2 HEADERS and DATA on stream 1

flows.title: Resumption with 0-RTT early data
flows.summary: A later connection uses the ticket from the full handshake: no certificate this time, and the request rides in the first flight, so the response is back after one round trip. The last step shows what changes if the server says no to early data.

steps.label: Load the ticket, derive early keys
steps.detail: Hours later the browser opens a new TCP connection to www.example.com (already open here). It still holds the ticket from the full handshake, inside its lifetime, so it derives the PSK and from it the early secret, a binder key and the key for early data. It also makes a fresh x25519 key pair so the new session gets forward secrecy for everything after the first flight.

steps.label: ClientHello + early_data
steps.detail: The same kind of ClientHello as before, plus the ticket in pre_shared_key (always the last extension) and an early_data flag that says application data follows right away. The binder is an HMAC over this ClientHello with a key from the PSK, which proves the client really holds the PSK.

fields.name: key_share
fields.note: Lets the server mix in a fresh (EC)DHE, or fall back to a full handshake

fields.name: server_name, ALPN
fields.note: For 0-RTT the server must select the same ALPN as the original connection

fields.name: early_data
fields.note: A flag: 0-RTT application data follows this message

fields.name: pre_shared_key.identity
fields.note: obfuscated_ticket_age = ticket age in ms + ticket_age_add, mod 2^32

fields.name: pre_shared_key.binder
fields.note: Over the ClientHello up to the binders, keyed from binder_key

steps.label: (GET /) 0-RTT data
steps.detail: The request leaves right behind the ClientHello (delay 0) and reaches the server at 0.5 RTT, before any key exchange has finished. It is encrypted with keys from the PSK alone, so it is not forward secret, and an attacker who recorded these packets can send them again: nothing in TLS stops the same ClientHello and early data being replayed. Browsers only put idempotent requests here, like this GET.

fields.name: message
fields.note: HTTP/2 preface, SETTINGS and the request

fields.name: protection
fields.note: From client_early_traffic_secret

fields.name: size limit
fields.note: From the ticket

steps.label: Accept PSK and 0-RTT
steps.detail: The server decrypts the ticket, recomputes the PSK and checks the binder. To defend against replay it accepts the ticket only once (it records used tickets, or the ClientHello, in a store shared by its servers) and only if the ticket age the client claims fits the time since it was issued, within a small window. The version, cipher suite and ALPN match the original session, so it accepts early data.

fields.name: replay check
fields.value: ticket not seen before; age within the window
fields.note: RFC 8446 section 8: single-use tickets, ClientHello recording, freshness checks

steps.label: ServerHello + pre_shared_key
steps.detail: The server picks the first (only) PSK and adds its own key share, so the session keys come from the PSK and a fresh x25519 secret together. There is no certificate to send: holding the PSK already proves this is the server from the earlier connection.

fields.name: pre_shared_key
fields.note: To accept early data the server must pick the client's first PSK

steps.label: {EncryptedExtensions}
steps.detail: An early_data extension here means 'I accepted your early data'. With a PSK there is no Certificate or CertificateVerify, so the client goes straight from WAIT_EE to WAIT_FINISHED.

fields.name: early_data
fields.note: Present: 0-RTT accepted. Absent: rejected

steps.label: {Finished}
steps.detail: The server's Finished closes its flight. Because it accepted 0-RTT, it now reads the client's early data with the early data keys and waits for EndOfEarlyData (WAIT_EOED).

steps.label: Run the early GET
steps.detail: The server decrypts the early request and serves it at once. HTTP can mark such requests (RFC 8470: an Early-Data header to the origin, and 425 Too Early to make the client retry after the handshake) so an application can refuse anything not safe to replay.

fields.name: if not safe
fields.note: RFC 8470: the client then repeats it after the handshake

steps.label: [200 OK]
steps.detail: The response goes right behind the server's Finished, with application keys, and reaches the client at 1 RTT. A full handshake would bring it at 2 RTT.

steps.label: Check Finished, derive app keys
steps.detail: The client checks the server's Finished; with a PSK this MAC is what authenticates the server. Then it derives the application keys.

steps.label: (EndOfEarlyData)
steps.detail: Sent because the server accepted early data: it marks the end of 0-RTT data and the switch from early data keys to handshake keys. It is the last thing sent with the early data keys. The server moves on through WAIT_FLIGHT2 to WAIT_FINISHED (no client certificate).

fields.name: message
fields.note: Handshake type end_of_early_data (5), an empty message

steps.label: {Finished}
steps.detail: The client's Finished, under handshake keys, right behind EndOfEarlyData. Both sides are CONNECTED, and later requests use the application keys, which do include the fresh x25519 secret.

steps.label: What if the server says no
steps.detail: Had the ticket been used before, been too old, or the server not wanted early data, its EncryptedExtensions would carry no early_data. The server then skips the early records (they fail to decrypt with handshake keys, up to max_early_data_size) and the client sends no EndOfEarlyData, sends its Finished and resends the GET with application keys. The response comes at 2 RTT, as in a full handshake, though resumption still skips the certificate. If the server rejects the PSK altogether it falls back to a full handshake using the client's key_share.

fields.name: EncryptedExtensions
fields.note: The rejection signal

fields.name: server
fields.value: skips early records that fail to decrypt

fields.name: client
fields.value: no EndOfEarlyData; resends GET after its Finished

flows.title: HelloRetryRequest: wrong key share guess
flows.summary: The client sends a key share only for x25519, but this server only allows P-256 (secp256r1). The server asks it to try again, which costs a full extra round trip.

steps.label: Guess x25519
steps.detail: The TCP connection is already open. The client lists x25519 and secp256r1 in supported_groups but, to keep the ClientHello small and save work, sends a key share only for x25519. This server is configured for P-256 only (for example a strict compliance setting).

steps.label: ClientHello (x25519 share)
steps.detail: The same ClientHello as in a full handshake.

steps.label: No usable key share
steps.detail: The server finds a group both support, secp256r1, but has no share for it, so it cannot compute a shared secret. Instead of failing it asks for another ClientHello. It replaces the first ClientHello in its transcript by a message_hash of it, so it can stay stateless if it wants (with a cookie).

fields.name: common group
fields.note: In the client's supported_groups, but not in its key_share

steps.label: HelloRetryRequest
steps.detail: A ServerHello with a special random value: the SHA-256 of the string "HelloRetryRequest". It names the group the client should use. Sending it puts the server back in START; receiving it puts the client back in START, and it arrives at 1 RTT with nothing negotiated yet.

fields.name: message
fields.note: Type server_hello (2) on the wire; recognised by its random

fields.name: random
fields.note: SHA-256("HelloRetryRequest"), fixed by RFC 8446 4.1.3

fields.name: cipher_suite
fields.note: The ServerHello must repeat this choice

fields.name: key_share
fields.note: Only the group, no share

steps.label: Make a P-256 key pair
steps.detail: The client checks that secp256r1 was in its supported_groups and was not already in its key_share (otherwise it must abort with illegal_parameter), then makes a P-256 key pair.

fields.name: public key
fields.note: Uncompressed point form, the only form TLS 1.3 uses

steps.label: ClientHello (P-256 share)
steps.detail: The second ClientHello is the first one with the key_share replaced (and a cookie added if the server sent one). It must not offer early_data. It leaves at 1 RTT and arrives at 1.5.

steps.label: Pick parameters, derive keys
steps.detail: Now the server has a share it can use. From here it is the full handshake, one round trip late.

steps.label: ServerHello
steps.detail: Arrives at 2 RTT. The client checks the cipher suite is the one the HelloRetryRequest named.

steps.label: {EncryptedExtensions}
steps.detail: As in the full handshake.

steps.label: {Certificate}
steps.detail: As in the full handshake.

steps.label: {CertificateVerify}
steps.detail: The signed transcript now covers the message_hash of the first ClientHello, the HelloRetryRequest and everything after.

steps.label: {Finished}
steps.detail: The server's flight ends; with no client certificate it goes through WAIT_FLIGHT2 to WAIT_FINISHED.

steps.label: Check everything
steps.detail: Chain, name, dates, signature and Finished, as in the full handshake (condensed into one step here).

steps.label: {Finished}
steps.detail: The client is CONNECTED at 2 RTT instead of 1. On a 100 ms path that is 100 ms more, on every new connection to this server, which is why clients send shares for the groups servers almost always take (x25519, and some also send secp256r1). The RFC also lets a client use what it learned from a completed handshake to pick its key_share for the next connection.

steps.label: [GET /]
steps.detail: The request goes with the Finished and arrives at 2.5 RTT.

steps.label: [200 OK]
steps.detail: Back at 3 RTT, one more than without the retry.

flows.title: Certificate not trusted
flows.summary: The server presents a chain that ends at a CA the browser does not trust. The client aborts with a fatal alert, and no request is ever sent.

steps.label: ClientHello
steps.detail: The TCP connection is already open, and the hello is the same as in a full handshake.

steps.label: Pick parameters, derive keys
steps.detail: Nothing unusual on the server side. Its certificate was issued by a private, in-house CA, which is fine for its own machines but not in any browser's trust store.

steps.label: ServerHello
steps.detail: Arrives at 1 RTT; the client derives handshake keys.

steps.label: {EncryptedExtensions}
steps.detail: As in the full handshake.

steps.label: {Certificate}
steps.detail: The chain the server sends: the leaf for www.example.com and the in-house intermediate.

fields.name: certificate_list[0]
fields.value: CN=www.example.com, issued by Example Internal CA

fields.name: certificate_list[1]
fields.value: Example Internal CA, issued by Example Internal Root

steps.label: {CertificateVerify}
steps.detail: Already in flight with the rest of the server's first flight. The client never reads it.

steps.label: {Finished}
steps.detail: Also in flight, also never read. The server waits for the client's Finished.

steps.label: No path to a trusted root
steps.detail: Processing the Certificate, the client tries to build a path from the leaf to a root in its trust store and cannot: Example Internal Root is not there. A name mismatch (a leaf whose subjectAltName does not cover www.example.com) or an expired certificate fails here too. The client stops processing the server's flight; it never reaches WAIT_CV.

fields.name: path
fields.value: leaf -> Example Internal CA -> Example Internal Root (not trusted)

steps.label: {Alert: unknown_ca}
steps.detail: The client sends a fatal alert and closes the connection. Every error alert is fatal in TLS 1.3. It already has handshake keys, and the RFC says it SHOULD use them for alerts after the ServerHello, so the alert is encrypted. No request was sent: the URL path, cookies and headers never left the browser.

fields.name: description
fields.note: RFC 8446 6.2: a chain was received but could not be matched with a known trust anchor. An expired certificate would be certificate_expired (45)

steps.label: Close and show an error
steps.detail: The client closes the TCP connection. The browser shows a full-page certificate error (Chrome: NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID). If the site is on the HSTS list the user cannot click through it.

notes.text: Forward secrecy: every full handshake uses a fresh (EC)DHE key pair on both sides, and the private halves are thrown away. The certificate's private key only signs; it never decrypts anything. So stealing that key later does not decrypt traffic someone recorded today. TLS 1.3 removed static RSA key exchange, which had no forward secrecy.

What an observer still sees: the server's IP address, the SNI name in the ClientHello, the ALPN list, record sizes and timing. The certificate is encrypted in TLS 1.3 (it was plaintext in 1.2). Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) hides the real SNI too: the client encrypts an inner ClientHello with a key the site publishes in DNS, and the outer ClientHello shows only a shared name of the provider.

Middlebox compatibility mode (RFC 8446 appendix D.4): many firewalls broke when they saw a handshake they did not recognise, so TLS 1.3 dresses up as TLS 1.2 resumption. The ClientHello says version 0x0303 and carries a 32-byte session ID, and each side sends a dummy change_cipher_spec record, which the peer ignores. Not drawn in the timelines.

Downgrade protection: a TLS 1.3 server that ends up negotiating TLS 1.2 or lower puts DOWNGRD (44 4F 57 4E 47 52 44) and 01 or 00 in the last 8 bytes of its ServerHello random. A TLS 1.3 client that sees this while negotiating an older version aborts, so an attacker cannot quietly strip supported_versions to force TLS 1.2. The random is covered by the older versions' signatures, so it cannot be edited back.

Certificate transparency and OCSP: publicly trusted certificates are logged in public CT logs (RFC 6962), and browsers like Chrome require proof of logging (signed certificate timestamps), so a CA cannot quietly issue a certificate for your name. OCSP stapling lets the server attach a fresh signed 'not revoked' answer from the CA inside the Certificate message, so the client does not have to ask the CA itself.

0-RTT trades safety for a round trip. Early data is encrypted only with keys from the PSK, so it is not forward secret, and an attacker can replay it, even to a different server of the same site. Servers limit the damage with single-use tickets or a ClientHello record within a short freshness window, and applications only accept idempotent requests in it (HTTP marks them and can answer 425 Too Early).

questions.q: Why does a TLS 1.3 handshake take one round trip when TLS 1.2 took two?
questions.a: In TLS 1.2 the first round trip only agreed on the algorithms, and the key exchange happened in the second, so the client could send its request after 2 RTT. In TLS 1.3 the client guesses the group and sends its key share in the ClientHello, so the server can complete the key exchange in its first answer and send its certificate, signature and Finished already encrypted. The client can then send Finished and its request together after 1 RTT. If the guess is wrong, a HelloRetryRequest costs the extra round trip after all.

questions.q: What does forward secrecy buy you, and how does TLS 1.3 get it?
questions.a: If the server's private key is stolen later, recorded past traffic stays secret. TLS 1.3 gets it because every full handshake uses ephemeral (EC)DHE: both sides make fresh key pairs, derive the session keys from the shared secret and throw the private halves away. The certificate key only signs the handshake. TLS 1.2 still allowed RSA key exchange, where the client encrypted the secret to the certificate's key, so a stolen key decrypted every recorded session. Note the exceptions: 0-RTT early data, and PSK-only resumption without (EC)DHE.

questions.q: 0-RTT saves a round trip on resumption. What does it risk, and how do you use it safely?
questions.a: Early data is encrypted only with keys from the resumption PSK, so it is not forward secret, and nothing in TLS stops an attacker from replaying the ClientHello and early data, possibly many times and to different servers of the same site. So only idempotent requests (a GET with no side effects) belong in it. Servers defend with single-use tickets or a record of recent ClientHellos within a short freshness window, and HTTP marks early requests so an application can answer 425 Too Early and make the client retry after the handshake.

questions.q: The connection is encrypted. What can a network observer still learn, and how does Encrypted Client Hello help?
questions.a: The server's IP address, the SNI in the plaintext ClientHello (so the exact site name, even on a shared IP), the ALPN offer, and the size and timing of the records. In TLS 1.3 the certificate is encrypted, so it no longer gives the name away, but SNI does. ECH encrypts an inner ClientHello, with the real SNI, to a public key the site publishes in DNS; the outer ClientHello shows only a shared name of the provider. It helps most when many sites sit behind the same provider, so the IP address does not identify the site either.

questions.q: How does the browser decide to trust the certificate it receives?
questions.a: It builds a chain from the leaf through the intermediates the server sent to a root already in its trust store, and checks each signature with the next certificate's public key. It checks that every certificate is within its validity dates, that the leaf's subjectAltName covers the host name it asked for, that the key usages allow server authentication, and whatever revocation and certificate transparency evidence its policy requires. Then CertificateVerify proves the server holds the leaf's private key, and Finished ties it all to this handshake. Any failure ends in a fatal alert such as unknown_ca.

questions.q: What does mutual TLS add to this handshake?
questions.a: The server adds a CertificateRequest to its encrypted flight, after EncryptedExtensions, and the client answers with its own Certificate and CertificateVerify before its Finished. So it costs no extra round trip, only more bytes and a signature on each side. The server then knows which client it is talking to from the handshake itself, which is common between services. Until it has checked the client's flight, any 0.5-RTT data the server sends goes to a peer it has not yet authenticated.
